Good morning. Let me give you an overview first, and then the numbers. There are three things, and I will finish with what I need from you. The headline number is four point two per cent. For context, the baseline was three point one, and this is the largest book in the region and the fastest growing, so a number that looks bad in a table looks different once you know that. Second, why it moved. It moved because the April cohort reached its third payment this month. We ruled out the model in the first hour, so the policy was the next place to look. Third, the decision. We are tightening the rule again, and the trade-off is two quarters of growth. If you remember one thing from this, the takeaway is that the rate is one cohort, not the portfolio, and it is already handled. What I need from you is one signature from risk this week. That is the only blocker.

When somebody presents in a second language, the first thing they lose is not the vocabulary. It is the structure. The signals go: the sentence that tells the room what is coming, the one that says how many parts there are, the one that says this is the end. All the information is still there, and the room still cannot follow it, and the presenter walks out thinking their English is the problem. Two things fix most of it. The first is slower. The people who sound most senior in any language are the ones who leave a silence between the parts, and a second language gives you a perfect excuse to take that silence. The second is this: prepare two sentences word for word, the first one and the last one. Not the whole thing. Two. Everything in the middle can be improvised, because you know the content better than anybody in the room. It is the beginning and the end where nerves take the words away, so those are the ones you write down.
